candidates.name: Passengers on the Bus
candidates.description: ACT metaphor: you are the bus driver, unwanted thoughts/feelings are rowdy passengers. You can drive toward your values without obeying them. Core self-as-context intervention.

candidates.name: Quicksand
candidates.description: ACT metaphor: struggling with difficult feelings makes you sink deeper, like struggling in quicksand. Acceptance (spreading out, going still) is counter-intuitive but effective.

candidates.name: Tug of War with a Monster
candidates.description: ACT metaphor: you are in a tug-of-war with a monster (your pain) over a bottomless pit. The solution is not to pull harder but to drop the rope entirely.

candidates.name: Leaves on a Stream
candidates.description: ACT defusion exercise: visualize placing each thought on a leaf and watching it float downstream. Teaches non-attachment to thoughts without suppressing them.

candidates.name: The Chessboard
candidates.description: ACT self-as-context metaphor: you are not the chess pieces (thoughts, feelings) but the board itself. The board holds all pieces without being threatened by any of them.

candidates.name: The Sky and the Weather
candidates.description: ACT self-as-context metaphor: you are the sky, your emotions are the weather. Weather changes constantly but the sky remains. Distinguishes transient experience from stable self.

candidates.name: The Unwelcome Party Guest
candidates.description: ACT acceptance metaphor: difficult emotions are like uninvited guests at your party. Trying to throw them out ruins the party for everyone. Better to let them stay while you host.

candidates.name: The Struggle Switch
candidates.description: ACT metaphor by Russ Harris: imagine a switch at the back of your mind. When ON, you struggle with every uncomfortable feeling, creating suffering on top of pain. Turning it OFF is acceptance.

candidates.name: Clean Pain vs Dirty Pain
candidates.description: ACT distinction borrowing from cleanliness/contamination: clean pain is unavoidable suffering; dirty pain is the contaminated layer we add by struggling with clean pain (anxiety about anxiety, guilt about guilt). The clean/dirty metaphor imports purity logic into emotional processing.

candidates.name: The Mind as a Radio
candidates.description: ACT defusion metaphor: your mind is like a radio that plays negative commentary. You cannot turn it off, but you can turn down the volume and stop taking it literally.

candidates.name: The Values Compass
candidates.description: ACT values metaphor: values are like a compass pointing in a direction, not a destination you arrive at. You can always check your heading even when lost.

candidates.name: Dropping the Anchor
candidates.description: ACT grounding technique: in an emotional storm, drop an anchor. It does not stop the storm, but it holds you steady so you do not get swept away.

candidates.name: The Choice Point
candidates.description: ACT framework by Russ Harris: at any moment you are at a choice point between moving toward your values or away from them. Internal experiences show up but do not determine the choice.

candidates.name: The Finger Trap
candidates.description: ACT acceptance metaphor: like a Chinese finger trap, pulling harder (resisting) makes you more stuck. The counter-intuitive solution is to push inward (toward the discomfort).

candidates.name: Ball in a Pool
candidates.description: ACT acceptance metaphor: pushing a beach ball underwater takes constant effort, and it pops back up violently when you let go. Suppressing emotions works the same way.

candidates.name: Demons on the Boat
candidates.description: ACT variant of passengers on the bus: demons (painful emotions) threaten you on your boat, but if you stop fighting them and sail toward your values, they lose their power.

candidates.name: Hands as Thoughts
candidates.description: ACT defusion exercise: hold hands in front of face (fused with thoughts, cannot see). Slowly lower them (defusion). The thoughts are still there but no longer block your view.

candidates.name: Creative Hopelessness
candidates.description: ACT phase where the client recognizes that all their control strategies have failed. The 'creative' reframes hopelessness as generative (from art/creation): if fighting does not work, the void becomes space for something new.

candidates.name: Cognitive Defusion
candidates.description: ACT core process: thoughts are fused like a bomb fused to detonate. Defusion is removing the fuse -- the thought remains but loses its explosive power to control behavior.

candidates.name: Psychological Flexibility
candidates.description: ACT central construct: the mind can be rigid (brittle, breaking under pressure) or flexible (bending without breaking). The hexaflex model maps six processes that contribute to flexibility.

candidates.name: Externalizing the Problem
candidates.description: Michael White's narrative therapy technique: the person is not the problem; the problem is the problem. Separating identity from problem creates agency to resist it.

candidates.name: Re-Authoring
candidates.description: Narrative therapy: the client is the author of their life story, and dominant problem-saturated narratives can be rewritten by finding and amplifying unique outcomes that contradict the problem story.

candidates.name: Unique Outcomes
candidates.description: Narrative therapy (White and Epston): moments when the problem's influence was resisted or absent. These exceptions to the dominant story become seeds for an alternative narrative.

candidates.name: The Absent but Implicit
candidates.description: Narrative therapy (White): when someone expresses pain, there is an implicit value being violated. The therapist names what is absent (the cherished value) to connect pain to meaning.

candidates.name: Double Listening
candidates.description: Narrative therapy: simultaneously listening to the problem story AND the counter-story (values, skills, hopes) embedded within it. Requires hearing what is said AND what is not said.

candidates.name: Holding Space
candidates.description: Therapeutic stance rooted in Winnicott's 'holding' (1960), popularized by Heather Plett (2015): creating a container where someone can feel without being fixed. Has migrated into coaching, management, and UX. Doing less is doing more.

candidates.name: The Therapeutic Alliance
candidates.description: Bordin's concept: therapist and client form an alliance (military metaphor) with agreed goals, tasks, and emotional bond. Has migrated into UX ('user alliance') and management ('stakeholder alliance').

candidates.name: Rupture and Repair
candidates.description: Safran and Muran's concept: breakdowns in the therapeutic relationship are not failures but opportunities. A repaired alliance is stronger than one never ruptured. Migrated into relationship coaching and team dynamics.

candidates.name: Unconditional Positive Regard
candidates.description: Rogers' concept (developed by Standal, 1954): accepting the whole person without conditions. Borrows from economics -- 'unconditional' vs 'conditional' is transactional language; regard without exchange terms. Migrated into parenting, education, and management philosophy.

candidates.name: Transference
candidates.description: Freud's concept: feelings about past figures are transferred onto the therapist. The spatial metaphor (transfer as movement of emotional charge from one vessel to another) has become a general term for misplaced emotional reactions. Originally a neurologic term for displacement of energies.

candidates.name: Window of Tolerance
candidates.description: Dan Siegel's concept (1999): a window (bounded aperture) through which you can process experience. Too much arousal pushes you above (hyperarousal), too little below (hypoarousal). Widely adopted in trauma therapy and education.

candidates.name: Felt Sense
candidates.description: Gendlin's focusing concept (1978): a pre-verbal bodily knowing that is more than emotion and more than thought. The body knows before the mind articulates. Migrated into UX research and design thinking.

candidates.name: The Body Keeps the Score
candidates.description: Van der Kolk's metaphor (1994 article, 2014 book): trauma is tallied in the body like a ledger. The body is an accounting system that records what the mind tries to forget. Has reshaped trauma treatment and popular understanding.

candidates.name: The Inner Child
candidates.description: The adult self contains a child-self that still carries old wounds and needs. Rooted in Jung's divine child archetype. Therapeutic work involves reparenting this inner child. Widely used in self-help, coaching, IFS therapy, and pop psychology.

candidates.name: Shadow Work
candidates.description: Jung's concept: the shadow is the disowned part of the self, cast by the light of the persona. Originally from Nietzsche. Integrating (not eliminating) the shadow is the work. Has migrated into leadership development and pop psychology.

candidates.name: Defense Mechanisms
candidates.description: Freud's military metaphor, systematized by Anna Freud (1936): the ego deploys defensive fortifications (denial, projection, sublimation) against threatening impulses. The self is a fortress under siege from within.

candidates.name: The Presenting Problem
candidates.description: Clinical term with theatrical metaphor: the problem presents itself on stage, but the real issue is backstage. Distinction between manifest complaint and latent dynamics. Used in consulting and diagnostics.

candidates.name: Pendulation
candidates.description: Somatic Experiencing concept by Peter Levine: therapeutic oscillation between activation (trauma state) and resource (safety). Like a pendulum, the nervous system swings between states and finds equilibrium.

candidates.name: Titration
candidates.description: Somatic Experiencing: approaching trauma in small, measured doses like a chemist adding reagent drop by drop. Too much too fast overwhelms; the right amount allows processing.

candidates.name: Containment
candidates.description: Bion's concept: the therapist acts as a container for the client's unbearable emotions, metabolizing them and returning them in digestible form. Widely used in management (leader-as-container) and education.

candidates.name: Mirroring
candidates.description: Kohut's self psychology: the therapist (or parent) mirrors the client's experience back, providing the reflective surface needed for self-recognition. Migrated into coaching, active listening, and UX empathy.

candidates.name: Scaffolding in Therapy
candidates.description: Vygotsky-derived concept (Wood, Bruner, Ross 1976) applied to therapy: temporary support structures that enable the client to do work they cannot yet do alone. The scaffolding is removed as capacity grows. Distinct from the educational 'scaffolding' entry -- therapeutic application emphasizes relational support and graduated withdrawal.

candidates.name: Working Through
candidates.description: Freud's Durcharbeitung (1914): psychological change requires repeatedly working through (like kneading dough or working through rock) resistant material. Insight alone is not enough; the labor of repetition is required.
